message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This case rests on hard data rather than impressions. We used four months of badge records to measure how many people actually come in, and average combined occupancy of 166 fits within Central's 180 desks, so consolidation does not require any new space. We also asked staff directly, with a 76% response rate, and the survey supports Central as the preferred single location. The financial case is straightforward and conservative: the full annual cost of Salford is £593,000, and even after £490,000 of one-off refit and dilapidation costs we are ahead in year one and save over £3.6 million across the life of the Central lease. Beyond cost, there is a delivery benefit. Since Central's 2024 refurbishment, projects led from there have finished 12% faster against programme, and bringing the infrastructure division into that environment should extend the same gains to our largest projects. I believe this is a rare proposal that improves the firm's finances, its working environment and its delivery at once.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
Business Case: Consolidating into a Single Manchester Office
Pelham and Rowe Consulting Engineers, Property Committee, May 2026

1. Proposal
We propose to close our Salford Quays office when its lease breaks on 31 March 2027 and consolidate all Manchester staff into our Central office on King Street, which we hold on a lease to 2034. Central would be refitted with a higher proportion of collaboration space and shared desks.

2. Current position
Central has 180 desks and houses our building services, structures and business support teams. Salford Quays has 120 desks and houses the infrastructure division, which works mainly on large transport and utilities projects. Between them the two offices accommodate 290 Manchester-based staff.

Table 1. Desk occupancy, January to April 2026 (badge data)
Office | Desks | Average daily occupancy | Average occupancy on Tuesdays and Wednesdays
Central | 180 | 102 | 151
Salford Quays | 120 | 64 | 97
Combined | 300 | 166 | 248

Average combined daily occupancy of 166 fits comfortably within the 180 desks at Central. Hybrid working is now well established, with most staff in the office two or three days a week.

3. Staff views
We surveyed all Manchester staff in March 2026 (221 responses, 76%).

Table 2. Staff survey: preferred single office location
Preference | Share of respondents
Central (King Street) | 34%
Salford Quays | 41%
No preference | 25%

Most staff prefer the Central office, and the King Street location is better served by rail for staff commuting from outside the city. Some infrastructure staff raised concerns about the loss of their dedicated project rooms, which we address through the refit.

4. Collaboration benefits
Central was refurbished in 2024 with open collaboration areas and bookable project rooms. Since then, projects led from Central have been completed on average 12% faster against programme than projects led from Salford Quays. Co-locating all staff in the refurbished Central space should therefore speed up delivery across the firm, particularly on the infrastructure projects now run from Salford. Central's projects are mostly smaller building services and structural commissions with short programmes, while Salford leads multi-year infrastructure frameworks with many external stakeholders.

5. Costs and savings
Table 3. Annual cost of the Salford Quays office
Item | Annual cost
Rent | £410,000
Service charge | £95,000
Business rates | £88,000
Total | £593,000

One-off costs of consolidation are a refit of Central (£340,000) and dilapidations payable on leaving Salford (£150,000), a total of £490,000. In the first year, net savings are therefore £103,000, and from the second year onwards the full £593,000 a year is saved. Over the remaining seven years of the Central lease, the cumulative net saving is about £3.66 million.

6. Risks
Disruption during the move: the move would be phased over two weekends in March 2027, with IT services migrated in advance.
Client perception: some infrastructure clients are based near Salford Quays. Project teams will continue to work from client offices where needed.
Staff retention: a minority of staff may find the commute to King Street harder. HR will review individual cases and offer flexible start times.

7. Recommendation
Consolidation saves £593,000 a year once the move is complete, is supported by staff preferences, fits comfortably within Central's capacity on current occupancy, and brings our infrastructure teams into a space that has demonstrably improved project delivery. We recommend that the Committee approve serving notice on the Salford Quays lease and a refit budget of £340,000.
</document>
response:
# Review: Single Manchester Office business case

**Verdict: not ready to go to the Committee.** The recommendation is clearly stated, but three of its four supporting claims are contradicted by the document's own data. A decision-maker who reads the tables will notice this, and it will undermine the parts of the case that hold.

## Critical issues

**1. Central cannot hold peak occupancy.**
The case relies on average daily occupancy (166 vs 180 desks). Table 1 also shows Tuesday/Wednesday occupancy of **248**, which is **68 more people than Central's 180 desks** (about 38% over). With most staff in two or three days a week, those midweek peaks are the days that matter. On current patterns, Central would be over capacity two days every week.

The refit may make this worse, since adding collaboration space usually removes desks. The document doesn't give a post-refit desk count.

*Fix:* Size the case on peak demand. Then show how 248 people fit, through a post-refit desk count, managed attendance days, or extra space. Cost whichever you choose, and add this to the Risks section, where it is currently missing.

**2. The survey favours Salford, not Central.**
Table 2 shows Salford Quays at 41% and Central at 34%. The text says "most staff prefer the Central office," and the recommendation says the move "is supported by staff preferences." Neither statement is true. Salford is the plurality choice, and neither option has a majority.

*Fix:* Report the result accurately. If Central is still the right choice for rail access, lease length or cost, argue that openly and acknowledge that staff leaned the other way. Retention risk in Section 6 should also reflect that 41% preferred the office being closed, rather than "a minority."

**3. The 12% delivery gain is not a like-for-like comparison.**
Section 4 states that Central's projects are mostly small, short-programme commissions, while Salford runs multi-year infrastructure frameworks with many external stakeholders. Those portfolios would be expected to perform differently against programme regardless of the office. There is also no before/after comparison for Central itself. The data doesn't show the refurbishment caused anything, so "demonstrably improved project delivery" in the recommendation is not supported.

*Fix:* Either compare similar project types, or compare Central's performance before and after 2024. Otherwise, drop the claim or present collaboration as a hoped-for qualitative benefit.

## Other issues

**4. The approval request leaves out part of the one-off cost.** The recommendation asks for a £340,000 refit budget, but the case's own one-off total is £490,000, including £150,000 of dilapidations. The Committee should approve the full figure, plus any capacity solution arising from issue 1.

**5. The savings are gross, not net.** The arithmetic is correct (£593k − £490k = £103k in year one; £103k + 6 × £593k ≈ £3.66m). However, it assumes no extra running costs at Central from roughly 60% more people using it, such as utilities, cleaning, facilities and service charge changes. It also leaves out Salford costs other than rent, service charge and rates. "Conservative" may still be fair, but the case should say what is and isn't included. A discounted figure would also be normal for a seven-year projection.

**6. The notice deadline isn't stated.** The proposal depends on serving notice for a 31 March 2027 break, but the document doesn't give the notice period or deadline. Since the paper is dated May 2026, please confirm the break is still exercisable before this goes forward.

**7. Client proximity risk is thin.** Infrastructure is your largest-project division, and its clients are near Salford. "Teams will work from client offices" deserves a sentence on cost or travel impact.

## What holds up

- The financial arithmetic is correct, and the underlying saving is substantial.
- The 76% response rate is correctly calculated (221/290) and is a strong base.
- The longer Central lease and its rail access are legitimate reasons to prefer Central.

## Suggested revised recommendation (once the issues are fixed)

> Consolidation saves about £593,000 a year from 2028/29 (£X net of additional Central running costs). Peak midweek demand of 248 exceeds Central's capacity, so we propose [solution, cost]. Staff narrowly preferred Salford (41% vs 34%), but Central's longer lease and better rail access make it the better long-term base. We recommend the Committee approve serving notice on the Salford lease and one-off costs of £[490,000 + capacity solution].

A recommendation like that is a credible case. In its current form, the paper leans on capacity, staff support and delivery claims that the Committee can disprove from the tables in the same document.
